title: Breast Cancer Diagnosis With Explainable
abstract: Breast cancer is one of the most common malignancies afﬂicting women globally, necessitating the use of cutting-edge AI approaches in diagnostic procedures to improve patient outcomes drastically. However, one key difﬁculty with the most recent AI models is a lack of transparency, making it difﬁcult for medical practitioners to implement these technologies to increase diagnostic accuracy. Many explainable AI (XAI) solutions have been developed to overcome this issue. This survey focuses on applying XAI approaches in breast cancer detection and diagnosis, particularly emphasizing their role in increasing model transparency and clinical decision-making. The article also provides insights into the inherent biases in the most recent machine learning models towards speciﬁc XAI approaches, such as the compatibility of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) with visual explanation methods and tree-based models with feature signiﬁcance evaluations. Finally, the article covers the obstacles to using XAI technologies in clinical practice and the signiﬁcance of deﬁning standard measures for assessing their performance.

sections.label: I.
sections.title: INTRODUCTION
paragraphs: Breast cancer (BC) ranks as the predominant form of cancer in adults worldwide, with an alarming rate of over 2.3 million new cases each year, as reported by the World Health Organization (WHO) 2022 [1]. Breast cancer survival rates vary signiﬁcantly across the globe, with a majority of deaths occurring in low- and middle-income countries. Early detec- tion is crucial as it leads to a clinical cure rate of over 90%, but this decreases signiﬁcantly as the cancer progresses [2]. Integrating artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) techniques into breast cancer diagnosis can improve early diagnosis and patient outcomes. AI systems’ ability to analyze large datasets, recognize patterns, and perform predictive analysis can The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and approving it for publication was Juan Wang . Breast cancer is categorized into three primary groups that reﬂect the stage of the disease and the complexity of treatment. Primary breast cancer, which makes up 80% of cases, is found initially in the breast without having spread beyond the breast or the lymph nodes under the arms. Secondary breast cancer, constituting 14% of cases, involves cancer spreading to other parts of the body, such as the lungs, bones, or liver. The smallest group, which accounts for 6% of cases, includes those with both primary and secondary characteristics due to recurrence, indicating that the cancer has returned after treatment, either at the original site or elsewhere. The studies reviewed in this article are distributed according to the abovementioned categories. AI optimizes diagnostics and treatments by analyzing vast medical data, including Electronic Health Records (EHRs) and image data, to identify patterns and accurately predict outcomes. It aids in detecting diseases like cancer in medical images, enhancing diagnoses and patient outcomes. By analyzing medical history and genetic data, AI enables early disease detection and suggests preventive measures, improving patient care. Moreover, by automating routine tasks, AI reduces healthcare costs and streamlines workﬂows, allowing providers to focus on complex cases and improving patient access to care [4]. However, some limitations must be considered. One of the limitations is the inadequate diversity of the training data utilized. For instance, if the training data consists of images of breasts from only one ethnic group, it may not accurately identify cancer in breasts from other ethnic groups [5]. Moreover, the systems might lack clarity, posing a challenge for doctors to comprehend the reasoning guiding the system’s decision-making process. This lack of transparency could be troublesome in medical contexts, where human expertise and intuition are necessary for accurate diagnosis [6], [7]. To address these limitations, Explainable Artiﬁcial Intelli- gence (XAI) could be a promising approach that offers clear explanations of AI systems’ decision-making processes. This clarity increases trust in recommendations for both medical professionals and patients, aiding informed decision-making. Additionally, interpretability helps reduce false positives and negatives, enhancing accuracy and minimizing risks in diagnosis and treatment [8], [9], [10]. This article provides a comprehensive overview of XAI techniques leveraged for various state-of-the-art breast cancer detection applications. Examples of these XAI techniques include case-based rea- soning (CBR), visualization, and feature importance analysis. Additionally, the emphasis is on the main XAI methods discussed in the paper - LIME, SHAP, and GRAD CAM- rather than focusing on others. This article presents a systematic literature review (SLR) examining the use of Explainable Artiﬁcial Intelligence (XAI) strategies in breast-cancer detection and diagnosis. We evaluate how XAI methods enhance model transparency and trust in automated systems, identify prevailing gaps across existing studies, highlight promising future paths for XAI in medical imaging, and investigate the inﬂuence of XAI on clinical decision-making and patient outcomes. While prior reviews have focused on the broader appli- cation of XAI in medical imaging, this paper narrows the scope to breast-cancer diagnosis only. In doing so, our contributions are three-fold: (a) We present a novel mapping between explanation-methods, model types and bias sources (i.e., a bias/explanation-method/model-type matrix). (b) We conduct a quantitative meta-analysis of 44 selected studies, assessing patterns of explanation-method usage and model-explanation alignment. (c) We discussed about evaluation frameworks that brings together bias detection and fairness metrics, clinical workﬂow integration and usability considerations for XAI in the breast-cancer context. The structure of the article is as follows: Section II outlines the review methodology and protocol. Section III presents the meta-analysis of selected studies, including publication sources, citation trends, geographic distribution and dataset modalities. Section IV provides an overview of XAI techniques and analyzes their frequency of application across various machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models. Section V discusses the speciﬁc XAI methods utilized for explaining ML/DL models applied to primary and secondary breast-cancer detection. Section VI offers a comprehensive analysis of the most frequently employed XAI techniques and their implications, while Section VII concludes with a discussion of key implications and future research directions.

sections.label: II.
sections.title: REVIEW METHOD
paragraphs: This paper uses the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items on Systematic Reviews and Meta-analysis) [11], [12] model. As mentioned above, this SLR aims to identify and present literature on XAI in breast cancer detection and diagnosis, with a particular emphasis on their role in increasing model transparency, thus enhancing trust in automated detec- tion systems among healthcare professionals and patients. This study will examine different XAI methods, including model-agnostic and model-speciﬁc approaches, to assess their ability to enhance breast cancer detection accuracy. In summary, the objectives of this review are: 1) To identify, collect, and synthesize existing research on the application of XAI techniques in the detection and diagnosis of breast cancer. 2) To assess various XAI approaches, including both model-agnostic and model-speciﬁc techniques, in terms of their effectiveness in improving the transparency and diagnostic accuracy of ML and DL models used for breast cancer detection.

subsections.label: B.
subsections.title: CRITERIA FOR INCLUSION AND EXCLUSION
paragraphs: Setting precise inclusion and exclusion criteria guarantees that only pertinent articles on breast cancer diagnosis using XAI are included in this study. We focused on studies published in reputable journals from January 2019 to June 2025. Our initial search based on the listed keywords resulted in 6302 research articles (refer to Figure 1 for a complete overview of the selection process). After a thorough review of the articles, we excluded articles that were unrelated to an XAI but appeared in the search because of keyword match. Additionally, articles were also excluded based on duplicity and non-availability of full text.

paragraphs: To conduct this survey, our search strategy aimed to gather relevant research articles addressing the application of XAI in breast cancer detection. Both automatic and manual search methods were employed to ensure comprehensive coverage of the available literature. The automatic search was conducted using reputable databases known for hosting scholarly works related to XAI and healthcare, refer to Figure 1. These databases were selected for their extensive collection of relevant research articles in the ﬁeld. While other sources such as magazines, working papers, newspapers, books, and blogs contain valuable information, they were not included in this survey due to the lack of rigorous peer-review processes, which could potentially compromise the reliability and quality of the ﬁndings. XAI approaches have been developed to increase transparency and trust in model predictions as explained in Figure 6. This section presents a taxonomy of XAI methodolo- gies, focusing on the three most often used approaches: SHapley Additive Explanations (SHAP), Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME), and Gradient- weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM). A comprehensive taxonomy of XAI techniques is pre- sented in Figure 7. In general, XAI models can be categorized into two types, including intrinsic and post-hoc models. It is possible to explain and comprehend intrinsic models, also called transparent models. Typical examples of trans- parent models include linear regression, logistic regression, and decision trees [112]. On the other hand, post-hoc is categorized into model-speciﬁc and model-agnostic. XAI explanations can also be categorized into two main types based on their scope, which includes global and local. A global explanation offers a comprehensive overview of the entire model, while a local explanation focuses on a single prediction or output. subsections.label: A.
subsections.title: EVALUATION FRAMEWORKS AND METRICS FOR
paragraphs: EXPLAINABLE AI XAI seeks to bridge the gap between the opaque decision-making of AI models and the need for human interpretability, fostering trust and reliability in AI-driven systems. However, measuring the effectiveness of XAI requires a multifaceted approach that addresses both technical rigor and user-centric considerations. A robust evaluation framework ensures explanations are not only accurate and reliable but also actionable and comprehensible to diverse stakeholders. Measuring Explainable Artiﬁcial Intelligence (XAI) involves a multifaceted evaluation that balances technical accuracy with user-centric effectiveness, ensuring explana- tions are both reliable and actionable. Fidelity is a critical metric, assessing how well explanations mirror the model’s decision-making process. Methods such as Correlation Metrics and Fidelity Scores, like Mean Squared Error (MSE), compare explanations with model predictions to validate their accuracy. Stability and Consistency are equally important, as they measure whether explanations remain reliable under slight input changes. This can be evaluated through Variance Analysis and Consistency Scores, ensuring trust in the system. Another vital consideration is Computational Efﬁciency, which focuses on the time and resources needed to generate explanations. Tools like Runtime Analysis and Resource Utilization are used to assess whether the system is suitable for real-time or resource-constrained applications. Beyond technical metrics, Comprehensibility and Usability are central to the user experience. These are often measured using User Surveys, Think-Aloud Protocols, and the System Usability Scale (SUS) to gather feedback on the clarity, coherence, and satisfaction users derive from explanations. It achieves this by utilizing the gradients and feature maps speciﬁc to a given CNN to highlight regions of an input image that are most inﬂuential in the model’s prediction. This reliance on the internal structure of CNNs, particularly the gradients ﬂowing into the ﬁnal convolutional layers, makes Grad-CAM a model-speciﬁc method tailored to convolu- tional architectures. Consequently, it is not directly applicable to non-convolutional models, such as those handling tabular data. However, Grad-CAM is also model-agnostic in the sense that it can be applied across various CNN architectures without requiring modiﬁcations to each model’s speciﬁc design. This ﬂexibility allows it to be used with a wide range of CNN-based models, making it a versatile tool for interpreting and visualizing CNN decisions [115]. The mathematical foundation of Grad-CAM is based on the gradients of the target class with respect to the feature maps. These gradients indicate the importance of each feature map for the target prediction. subsections.title: COMPLEMENTARY XAI METHODS IN BREAST CANCER
paragraphs: RESEARCH Beyond the core XAI techniques previously discussed, other methods also offer valuable insights into making complex machine-learning models more interpretable. These methods include counterfactual explanations, Permutation Importance, and various others, each contributing uniquely to the landscape of explainable AI (XAI). For instance, Althoff et al. [81] and Lamy et al. [14] introduced a visual case-based reasoning (CBR) method that integrates visual algorithms to illustrate case similarities, enhancing user interpretation of recommendations. In the context of CBR, a case refers to a problem situation. Generally, CBR consists of a (p + 1)-dimensional space case database represented as X, where xi represents each case. Each xi has components in different dimension spaces A1, . . . , Ak, . . . , Ap and Y is the solution space associated with each case. The query case can be represented as q ∈ A1 × . . . × Ak × . . . × Ap This hierarchical process involves four key steps: retrieval, reuse, revision, and retention. Such a structured approach facilitates decision-making, as demonstrated in breast cancer therapy, where CBR helps simplify complex decisions and validate results against established guidelines. However, challenges persist, including accuracy limitations and sensitivity to high-dimensional data. Gu et al. [16] addressed some of these challenges by combining CBR with ensemble learning, utilizing XGBoost for predictions while leveraging CBR for explanations. While this approach enhances XAI, it remains reliant on existing techniques and could beneﬁt from incorporating more comprehensive attribute considerations. Permutation Importance (PIMP), introduced by Altmann et al. [83], assesses feature signiﬁcance by measur- ing performance degradation after shufﬂing feature values. Khater et al. [48] integrated PIMP with SHAP and Partial Dependence Plots (PDP) to identify key features in breast cancer detection, such as bare nuclei and clump thickness. PDP extends this analysis by illustrating how individual features inﬂuence predictions, offering a contrast to methods that solely highlight the most signiﬁcant features [84]. The use of PDP revealed the correlation between changes in tissue architecture and breast cancer progression, with particular emphasis on the relationship between tissue thickness and cell stickiness, as shown in Khater et al. [48]. Similarly, Tosun et al. [15] developed HistoMapr-Breast, an XAI-enabled application designed to visualize and identify regions of interest in breast core biopsies. This tool supports pathologists’ decision-making by incorporating XAI into pathology workﬂows, effectively addressing con- cerns related to transparency and safety. Layerwise Relevance Propagation (LRP) [82] interprets deep neural networks by tracing information from the output neurons back to the input layers. Binder et al. [72] applied LRP to identify critical image regions and molecular biomarkers relevant to breast cancer prognosis. Cherada et al. [21] expanded on this approach by employing Graph LRP to explain predictions from Graph-CNNs, revealing signiﬁcant genes associated with cancer. Furthermore, Amoroso et al. [30] proposed an XAI method based on Adaptive Dimension Reduction (ADR), speciﬁcally designed for breast cancer therapies. Their framework, which integrates clustering and dimensionality reduction, effectively identiﬁed critical clinical features and contributed to the development of oncological treatment strategies. Idrees et al. [35] introduced XAI algorithms to analyze potential biomarkers for breast cancer. Various classiﬁcation models were applied to anthropometric data from three studies [124], [125], [126], augmented with XAI models. The table also identiﬁes potential biases in certain deep learning models, revealing a tendency to favor speciﬁc explainability methods over others. This analysis aids in understanding the limitations and advantages of different XAI techniques across various contexts. To begin with, SHAP is model-agnostic, meaning it is not tied to any speciﬁc machine learning (ML) or deep learning (DL) model. Refer to Figure 8 for a visualization created by SHAP. This characteristic is advantageous because it allows SHAP values to be applied to any machine learning model, regardless of its architecture or underlying algorithms [128]. This ﬂexibility is particularly valuable for tasks involving model comparison, as it provides a consistent method for interpreting predictions and understanding model behavior. Furthermore, because SHAP values are independent of the speciﬁc model being used, they can be easily adapted when the model is updated or replaced. In a machine learning pipeline, where models are often reﬁned or replaced over time, SHAP’s ﬂexibility ensures that the explanations VOLUME 13, 2025 17 remain consistent and informative, requiring minimal effort to integrate with updated models [129]. The Shapley values also offer three valuable properties not found in other XAI methods [77], [131]. 1) SHAP values provide local accuracy, meaning they accurately capture the difference between the expected output of the model and the output for a speciﬁc instance of input data. This means they provide insights into how individual features contribute to each prediction. 2) If a feature is missing (i.e. not present in the input data), its attribution value in the SHAP analysis is set to zero, ensuring that the absence of a feature is appropriately accounted for in the explanation.

EXPLAINABILITY FOR TRANSFORMER- AND VISION-LANGUAGE CLINICAL AI As clinical AI increasingly adopts Vision Transformers (ViTs) and vision-language models (VLMs), evaluating explainability requires more than visually plausible outputs. Explanations must be decision-faithful, region-grounded, robust, and fully auditable, ensuring that model rationales can be rigorously veriﬁed and trusted. For ViTs, we advocate transformer-aware pipelines that pair LRP-style relevance propagation (to trace token→patch evidence) with attention rollout/ﬂow (to characterize cross-layer information ﬂow), and we insist that visualizations remain testable hypotheses. Concretely: validate saliency with deletion/insertion curves and sanity checks; run counterfactual/perturbation audits (blur, mask, out-paint, or clinically plausible replacements) to demonstrate necessity and sufﬁciency; and add concept-level probes to estimate causal effects of named ﬁndings. These steps directly address evidence that raw attention can mislead S. For CLIP (Contrastive Language–Image Pretraining) - style clinical models, make text/image alignment auditable by design: expose region concept grounding during zero/few-shot inference, enforce prompt governance (template libraries, ensembles, sensitivity/ablation tests), calibrate uncertainty before thresholding, and run stratiﬁed subgroup/shift audits (site, device, demographics) to surface shortcutting and bias prior to deployment building on medical VLM work such as MedCLIP and CheXzero [139], [140]. Additionally in order to align with governance frame- works, we can employ documenting method cards, model/data cards, immutable decision logs, and a post-market monitoring plan consistent with the EU AI Act’s transparency and monitoring duties [141], the FDA/Health Canada/MHRA GMLP and Transparency principles [142], [143], ISO/IEC 23894 risk management [144], and IMDRF SaMD clinical evaluation [145]; report prospective studies under SPIRIT- AI/CONSORT-AI [146], [147]. The result is not prettier heatmaps, but a veriﬁable chain from evidence to decision that regulators, clinicians, and patients can inspect and trust.

subsections.title: OBSTACLES TO CLINICAL ADOPTION AND
paragraphs: STANDARDISED EVALUATION OF XAI IN BREAST CANCER DIAGNOSIS Despite the substantial promise of explainable artiﬁcial intelligence (XAI) in breast cancer diagnostics, signiﬁcant challenges persist on the path from research prototypes to routine clinical implementation. A key challenge is the lack of standardised evaluation frameworks: while many studies report model accuracy, far fewer assess how well explanations support human decision-making, inter-operator consistency, or workﬂow integration. Reviews of XAI evaluation methods in healthcare highlight that many papers rely on anecdotal evidence or bespoke user studies, and only a minority adopt shared frameworks, thereby limiting cross study comparability and trust in explanation outputs [148], [149], [150]. In the speciﬁc domain of breast-cancer diagnosis, this evaluation gap undermines study comparability, reduces clin- ician conﬁdence in explanation tools, and limits replicability of results. Another major barrier is the limited real-world valida- tion and generalisability of current XAI systems. Many breast-cancer detection studies rely on retrospective or single centre datasets with homogeneous populations or imaging devices, raising questions about external validity across breast densities, ethnic groups, or device vendors [151], [152]. Without thorough multi centre validation and diverse cohorts, even technically advanced XAI tools may fail when transferred to real-world clinical settings. Third, there is an inherent trade-off between explainability, accuracy and bias. Complex deep-learning models (such as convolutional neural networks) may yield high diagnostic performance but require post-hoc explanation tools whose ﬁdelity is not always guaranteed; conversely, simpler models VOLUME 13, 2025 21 may be interpretable but less robust. Many tree-based models are paired with SHAP/LIME, while CNN-based image models often rely on saliency maps reﬂecting a bias in model-explanation matching that our survey also revealed. Furthermore, if training data lacks diversity, explanation methods may systematically emphasise features pertinent in one domain but not in others, thereby embedding fairness risks [153]. Even when explanations are generated, the interpretability and usability of those explanations for end-users (clinicians, pathologists) remain under-explored. For example, a heat- map produced by Grad-CAM may appear intuitive, yet unless validated to correspond to a clinically-relevant patho- logical landmark, the clinician may ignore or mistrust it. Human-centred evaluation studies show wide variation in clinician comprehension and trust of different explanation formats, emphasising the need for user centric design and training [149]. Finally, workﬂow integration, ethical and regulatory issues present additional hurdles. Deploying an XAI enabled system in radiology or pathology services requires alignment with existing PACS/EHR systems, audit trails, clinician account- ability and clear responsibility when AI recommendations (and explanations) are delivered. Reviews of AI in screening note that regulatory, ethical and governance frameworks are still emergent and must evolve to support XAI-enabled clinical care [154], [155]. The deployment of such AI systems raises questions about liability, informed consent, transparency, and data-fairness especially in high-stakes domains such as breast-cancer diagnosis. In light of these gaps, recent literature suggests several strategic directions: • Develop and adopt clinically-oriented, standardised evaluation metrics and benchmark frameworks for XAI in breast-cancer diagnostics. The literature strongly emphasises that without such metrics—covering ﬁdelity, stability, usability and domain relevance XAI explanations cannot be reliably compared or trusted across studies [148]. • Expand multi centre, multi-modality and population- diverse validation studies to establish generalisability and fairness. Many XAI systems to date rely on single centre or homogeneous datasets; broad validation is required to ensure robustness across devices, modalities and patient populations [153]. • Design human-in-the-loop, workﬂow-embedded eval- uations, where clinicians interact with the AI + XAI system and their decision-making, trust and outcomes are formally measured. Human AI collaboration is now identiﬁed as a key element of trustworthy implementation [156]. • Tailor explanation methods to match the user group (radiologist, pathologist, oncologist) and the model type (tree-based, CNN, multimodal). Explanation formats that are technically accurate but misaligned to the FIGURE 9. Without careful attention to fairness of explanations, lia- bility, informed consent and auditability, XAI-enabled tools may fail regulatory or ethical acceptability even if technically accurate [157].

subsections.title: BRIDGING BIAS DISCOVERY TO CLINICAL IMPACT AND
paragraphs: MITIGATION Beyond identifying methodological and data-centric biases, it is crucial to understand how these biases manifest in clinical workﬂows. For instance, spurious correlations in imaging datasets such as scanner artefacts, skin markers or acquisition metadata inadvertently correlated with malignancy labels can lead XAI models to focus on non-pathological cues. Clinically, such biases may distort malignancy estimation and inﬂuence biopsy decisions, thereby impacting patient safety and diagnostic conﬁdence. Recent work emphasises that bias is a systemic concern at every stage of AI for medical imaging, from data sampling to deployment, making proactive detection and correction essential [158]. Moreover, frameworks like the ‘‘Reveal to Revise’’ life-cycle explicitly combine explanation-based bias identiﬁcation with model revision and re-evaluation, demonstrating how counterfactual testing, feature sensitivity analysis or domain-adversarial methods can attenuate spurious dependencies [159]. Embed- ding such mitigation mechanisms into model development and explanation evaluation therefore closes the translational loop from bias discovery to clinical practice, improving diagnostic robustness and enhancing clinician trust in XAI systems. Future work should extend these strategies through clinician-in-the-loop bias audits and post-deployment mon- 22 VOLUME 13, 2025 S. Bai et al.: Breast Cancer Diagnosis With XAI: Uncovering Strengths and Biases itoring to ensure sustained fairness and reliability across diverse patient populations. To support the translation of XAI into breast-cancer diagnostics, we propose an evaluation framework (shown in Figure 9 composed of four inter-linked domains: • Technical & Fidelity: Assess how well explanations mirror the model’s internal reasoning (e.g., ﬁdelity, stability, runtime) and whether explanation methods reveal model errors or biases. • Fairness & Bias-Detection: Quantify and mitigate bias sources (e.g., dataset imbalance, device shift, spurious correlations), evaluate cross-population robustness, and measure fairness of explanations across sub-groups. • Usability & Clinician Trust: Capture human centred metrics of how easily clinicians understand and act on explanations (e.g., usability scales, think-aloud proto- cols, decision-error reduction, trust/conﬁdence metrics). • Workﬂow & Clinical Integration: Evaluate how the XAI system embeds into real-world clinical workﬂows: interoperability with PACS/EHR, audit-trail readi- ness, clinician AI collaboration, and regulatory/ethical readiness. If these pathways are followed, the transition of XAI from promising research prototypes into trustworthy clinical tools for breast cancer diagnosis becomes far more likely.

sections.title: CONCLUSION
paragraphs: XAI plays a crucial role in evaluating model performance, which is essential for optimizing accuracy and reliability in practical applications. Beyond performance, it is imperative to assess the impact of XAI on user trust and comprehension. As AI technologies become increasingly integrated into healthcare, ensuring their transparency and interpretability S. Bai et al.: Breast Cancer Diagnosis With XAI: Uncovering Strengths and Biases is vital for fostering trust among medical practitioners and patients. Integrating various XAI approaches, however, presents signiﬁcant challenges, particularly in comparative analysis and generalization across diverse scenarios. This complexity highlights the need for a robust framework to evaluate these models comprehensively. Establishing standardized evaluation metrics is critical, as they provide consistent and reliable measures of effectiveness in clinical settings. These metrics should not only assess the accuracy and efﬁciency of XAI applications but also evaluate the quality of the explanations in terms of relevance, complete- ness, and consistency. Moreover, the integration of XAI into clinical workﬂows can advance personalized medicine. By offering tailored explanations, XAI can help clinicians understand the reasoning behind speciﬁc diagnostic or treatment decisions, which is particularly important in com- plex cases like breast cancer, where patient-speciﬁc factors signiﬁcantly inﬂuence outcomes. In addition to technical advancements, addressing the ethical implications of using AI in breast cancer diagnosis is imperative. The deployment of AI models in clinical settings must be guided by rigorous ethical standards to ensure patient privacy, data security, and equitable access to healthcare beneﬁts. Transparency in AI decision-making, achieved through XAI techniques, not only enhances trust among healthcare professionals and patients but also mitigates biases that may stem from non-representative training data.
